d89d8d236979.t: The phrase 'attraction, not promotion' is a cornerstone of how we carry the message. As Bill W. wrote in the Twelve Traditions, 'Our public relations policy is based on attraction rather than promotion' <0>[Page 564]</0>. This means we don't sell AA or push it on anyone. Instead, we live the program so fully that others see the peace and freedom we've found, and they want what we have. The Big Book tells us, 'Practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics' <1>[Page 89]</1>. When we focus on helping another sufferer, we stay sober and become living examples. Promotion—using big talk, gimmicks, or pressure—only repels those still struggling. Attraction comes from a changed life, one that demonstrates the promises: 'We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves' <2>[Page 84]</2>. So I ask myself daily: am I living in a way that draws others to this way of life, or am I just talking about it?

7142256d8b3c.t: Ah, my friend, complacency is the quiet thief of sobriety. The Big Book reminds us that our condition is cunning, baffling, and powerful — and that we are never fully cured. As it says on page 85: 'We are not cured of alcoholism. What we really have is a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition.' <0>[Page 85]</0> That daily reprieve means we never graduate from the program. The moment we think we've got it licked, we're in danger. I've seen many a sober alcoholic slip back into the drink because they stopped doing the very things that kept them sober — the meetings, the steps, the service. The book warns on page 33: 'There is a solution. Almost none of us liked the self-searching, the leveling of our pride, the confession of shortcomings which the process requires for its successful consummation.' <1>[Page 33]</1> But that self-searching is the lifeblood of recovery. Lest we become complacent, we must keep coming back, keep working the steps, and keep carrying the message to the still-suffering alcoholic. That's not a burden — it's our greatest protection.

8b17287177c3.t: The theme 'Fixing Me, Not You' cuts to the heart of the AA program. We alcoholics often arrived pointing fingers—blaming spouses, jobs, or a cruel world for our drinking. But the Big Book’s radical idea is that the real problem lives inside us. As it says, we must 'truly wish to be rid of [our] besetting faults' <0>[Page 76]</0>. Step Four is a fearless moral inventory of ourselves, not a critique of others <1>[Page 64]</1>. The Ninth Step promise that 'we will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' <2>[Page 83]</2> only comes when we stop fixing others and start working on our own character defects. This shift is the foundation of lasting sobriety: we are the ones who need changing. When we focus on our own growth, resentment dissolves and we become useful to others.

We thought we could run the show, that our will was supreme. But Step 2 invites us to 'come to believe that a Power greater than ourselves could restore us to sanity.' That Power—whatever we understand it to be—becomes our ultimate authority, not our own ego. On page 60, Step 3 says we 'made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him.' This is where we stop playing god. It's a surrender, but a liberating one. The Big Book's clear message is that our self-will got us drunk; turning to a Higher Power keeps us sober. This doesn't mean we become passive—we still act, but we seek guidance and align our actions with that authority. The result? A daily reprieve from alcoholism (page 85) based on our spiritual condition.

The Promises on pages 83-84 are the same today as when they were written — that’s the power of an unbroken tradition. You don’t have to reinvent the wheel; you just have to pick it up and pass it on.

The Big Book promises in the Promises that 'We will know a new freedom and a new happiness... We will be amazed before we are half through. We are going to know a new peace...' <0>[Page 83-84]</0>. What we really have is a daily reprieve...' <1>[Page 85]</1>—each day's serenity is a gift we receive by working our program, not by waiting for perfect calm. The storm may rage around us, but inside we can carry God's peace, one day at a time.

7a5d942ca18c.t: Ah, 'Live and let live' — a simple phrase, but it goes straight to the heart of our recovery. The Big Book first uses it in Chapter Two, where it says of the alcoholic: 'He must decide to live and let live, or he will die' <0>[Page 19]</0>. That's a stark choice: let go of trying to control others or be destroyed by resentment. Later, in Chapter Seven, we’re told we don't have to be 'a busybody' — we can trust that each person's journey is their own <1>[Page 98]</1>. This is the essence of tolerance: we stop trying to fix, change, or manage the people around us. Instead, we focus on our own side of the street.

3d86a55de0bf.t: When the Promises say we will 'intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' <0>[Page 83-84]</0>, that's the fruit of letting live. We no longer need to force outcomes or judge others' paths. We simply offer love and acceptance, knowing that our Higher Power is in charge of everyone's recovery — not us. Live and let live isn't passive; it's an active practice of trust and humility. It frees us from the exhausting job of playing God.

e20512b6633c.t: Avoiding controversy in recovery isn't about being a doormat—it's about guarding your sobriety. The Big Book warns that we cannot afford to be 'a martyr trying to get sympathy' or 'a hothead bent on having the last word' <0>[Page 70]</0>. Resentments are the 'number one offender' that can destroy us <1>[Page 64]</1>, and getting tangled in disputes is a sure way to build them. Instead, we practice self-restraint and tolerance, knowing that 'we are not to be the aggressor' <2>[Page 67]</2>. This doesn't mean we never disagree—it means we choose peace over being right, because our life depends on it. By steering clear of unnecessary conflict, we preserve the serenity our program has given us, and we stay fit to carry the message to others.

As we work Steps Four through Seven, we let go of old ideas and defects—those ‘twisted’ parts of us that block God’s light <1>[Page 68]</1>. The promise? ‘We will suddenly realize that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves’ <2>[Page 84]</2>. Pruning hurts sometimes, but it makes way for new life—the life of freedom and service.

051f8b248cec.t: Ah, 'yesterday's baggage' — that's a wonderful way to describe the weight we carry until the Steps teach us to set it down. In the Big Book, we read: 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it' <0>[Page 83]</0>. This isn't about pretending the past didn't happen — it's about packing it in a way that doesn't weigh us down. Resentments, fears, and regrets are the heaviest luggage we carry. Through the Fourth and Fifth Steps, we unpack each item and learn that God's forgiveness is real. The Promises assure us that 'we will be amazed before we are half through' <1>[Page 83]</1> with this process. Yesterday's baggage becomes today's lesson, not today's burden. And remember, we only get a daily reprieve <2>[Page 85]</2> from alcoholism. So each morning, we choose to leave yesterday's trunk on the platform and walk forward with just enough for today. That's the grace of this program.

9fe32e3f9fd7.t: Willingness to grow is the heartbeat of recovery. In the Big Book, we read that 'we must be entirely ready to have God remove all these defects of character' <0>[Page 76]</0>. That readiness isn't passive—it's an active, daily choice to say "I'm willing to let go of fear, resentment, and self-will, and let something new grow in their place." Step 6 and 7 are really about this: we can't force change, but we can cultivate the willingness that invites it.

4eef30e88dee.t: Growth in AA isn't about becoming perfect; it's about becoming whole. The Promises remind us that 'we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' <0>[Page 84]</0>. That kind of wisdom comes from practice, from making mistakes and getting back up. But it starts with a simple prayer: 'Take away my difficulties, that victory over them may bear witness...' <1>[Page 76]</1>. Willingness to grow means trusting the process, even when we can't see the outcome.

b4b368504fd2.t: So what does this look like today? Maybe it's asking for help when you'd rather pretend you're fine. Maybe it's reading the Big Book with an open mind instead of a critical one. Willingness is a muscle—the more you use it, the stronger it gets. And it's never too late to start flexing.

3d14567711d4.t: Recovery by proxy is a charming notion, but a dangerous one. The Big Book makes clear that each alcoholic must take his own journey. In the Doctor's Opinion, we read that the alcoholic 'cannot recover unless he wants to' [xxviii]. No amount of good intentions from others can substitute for that inner willingness. The program is not something we do for someone else — it is something we do with the help of God and our fellow alcoholics. Chapter 7 tells us that when we work with others, we 'carry the message' <0>[Page 89]</0>, but we cannot carry their recovery. That burden must be shouldered alone, one step at a time. Trying to recover by proxy is like trying to eat for someone else — it simply doesn't work. The Promises on pages 83-84 are for those who 'have humbly asked Him to remove our shortcomings' — a personal act, not a delegated one.

12f5a2185677.t: When we approach recovery with reservation, we hold back a piece of ourselves—a bit of fear, a shred of ego, a secret plan to drink again. The Big Book says on page 74, 'We must be entirely honest with somebody if we expect to live long or happily.' That honesty must be total, without any hidden corners. Giving ourselves fully to the Steps, starting with Step Three—'made a decision to turn our will and our life over to the care of God as we understood Him' <0>[Page 59]</0>—requires letting go of every mental escape hatch. On page 84, the Promises tell us 'we have ceased fighting anything or anyone—even alcohol.' That ceasefire only comes when we surrender without condition. Half measures availed us nothing <1>[Page 70]</1>. The freedom we find is directly proportional to the completeness of our surrender.

9d348b92954e.t: Recovery Einstein's Big Book perspective on the AA Daily Reflection for September 29.

c0288ac06c6a.t: The phrase 'exactly alike' captures a profound truth about our condition. On page 30, the Big Book says, 'We are not so much alike as we think we are, but we are exactly alike in that we have lost the power of choice in drink.' This is the great equalizer—regardless of background, drinking history, or personality, every alcoholic shares this singular loss of control. It’s not about how much we drank or how low we sank; it’s that when we start, we cannot reliably stop. Recognizing this sameness breaks down the walls of isolation and shame. We realize we’re not unique in our suffering—we’re just like every other alcoholic. And that common ground is where recovery begins. On page 17, we read that the alcoholic is an extreme example of self-will run riot, but the solution is equally universal: a spiritual awakening that can happen to anyone willing to work the Steps. So when you hear 'exactly alike,' let it remind you that your struggle is not yours alone—and neither is the hope found in these pages.

fad809fbb6e5.t: Where in your life have you felt uniquely hopeless, and how does knowing you are exactly alike with every recovering alcoholic free you from that isolation?

We don't wake up one day with a perfect life; we take small, steady actions—Step 9 amends, Step 10 inventories, Step 11 meditation—and suddenly realize we're living a life we never thought possible. The Promises on pages 83-84 aren't a distant reward; they're daily realities for those who 'clean house' and 'trust God.' Even the 'daily reprieve' on page 85 is part of building—it's the foundation that keeps us standing.

31bc4dbbfcc0.t: Recovery Einstein's Big Book perspective on the AA Daily Reflection for September 30.

52eec1f95d1c.t: The circle and triangle have long been symbols in AA, representing our threefold recovery: recovery, unity, and service—each essential for lasting sobriety. The circle reminds us that we are part of a fellowship where we ‘are not alone,’ and that our group conscience keeps us united. The triangle points to the three legacies: the Twelve Steps for personal recovery, the Twelve Traditions for group unity, and service to others. The Big Book emphasizes that ‘practical experience shows that nothing will so much insure immunity from drinking as intensive work with other alcoholics’ <0>[Page 89]</0>. This is service—the triangle’s top point. Without it, our recovery stalls. The Steps give us a design for living <1>[Page 28]</1>, and the Traditions protect our unity so that we can keep carrying the message. So the circle and triangle together mean that we stay sober by giving away what we have received, and we stay united by relying on principles, not personalities.

ea3ecfa795c7.t: Emotional balance for the recovering alcoholic is not the absence of strong feelings, but the ability to experience them without being overwhelmed. The Big Book promises that 'we will intuitively know how to handle situations which used to baffle us' <0>[Page 84]</0>, and this comes from working Steps 10 and 11. We learn to 'pause when agitated or doubtful' and ask for the right thought or action <1>[Page 87]</1>. This is the daily reprieve—not perfection, but a moment-by-moment reliance on our Higher Power to restore us to sanity <2>[Page 85]</2>. Emotional balance means we can feel anger, fear, or joy fully, yet not let those emotions drive us back to the bottle.

63df276756b6.t: Ah, seeking to remove threats to sobriety — that's the heart of daily maintenance. Read Einstein's Big Book take on today's AA reflection.

8ef4e2939ce1.t: Recovery Einstein's Big Book perspective on the AA Daily Reflection for September 6.

b4f7940d3724.t: Ah, seeking to remove threats to sobriety — that's the heart of daily maintenance. The Big Book tells us resentment is the "number one offender" that destroys more alcoholics than anything else <0>[Page 64]</0>. It's like a poison that, if left unchecked, will surely lead us back to the drink. But we're not left defenseless. The daily practice of the Tenth Step — continuing to take personal inventory and promptly admitting when we're wrong — keeps these threats at bay <1>[Page 84-85]</1>. We learn that our sobriety depends on maintaining a fit spiritual condition, and when we neglect that, old threats creep back in. The Promises assure us that we will "not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it" <2>[Page 83]</2>, but that comes from actively working the Steps and carrying the message to others. So removing threats isn't one dramatic act; it's the quiet, steady work of staying honest, humble, and connected to our Higher Power.

0412c6d80c23.t: When the Big Book says 'We asked His protection and care with complete abandon' <0>[Page 63]</0>, it isn't about asking God to keep us safe from external harm. It's about surrendering the illusion that we can manage our own lives. In recovery, we've seen where our best thinking got us—jails, institutions, or death. Asking for protection means praying for the strength to stay out of self-will and to trust a Power greater than ourselves with every detail of our day, just as the Third Step Prayer suggests. This is not a one-time request; it's a daily attitude of turning our will and our lives over to God's care <1>[Page 63]</1>, moment by moment. When we do that consistently, we find that God is doing for us what we could not do for ourselves <2>[Page 84]</2>, and that is the real protection—from the bondage of self and the obsession to drink.

d698b85f0dca.t: Opening new doors in recovery is about the promise of a new life that the Big Book describes. On page 83, it says, 'We will not regret the past nor wish to shut the door on it.' This doesn't mean we forget—it means we stop being prisoners of shame. The door to the past stays open behind us, but we're free to walk through new doors ahead. Chapter 6 promises that we will 'know a new freedom and a new happiness' <0>[Page 83]</0>. That freedom comes from working the Steps and carrying the message to others. Each time we help a still-suffering alcoholic, we open another door—not just for them, but for ourselves <1>[Page 89]</1>. The daily reprieve we receive <2>[Page 85]</2> is only as good as the action we take to keep walking through those new doors. So opening new doors means trusting that God, as we understand Him, will show us which door to open next—and having the courage to step through.
